Utilitarianism is a consequentialist ethical theory holding that the morally right action is the one that maximizes overall happiness or well-being for the greatest number of people. Founded by Jeremy Bentham and refined by John Stuart Mill in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, utilitarianism reduces ethics to a calculus of pleasure and pain, or more broadly, preference satisfaction and flourishing. Utilitarianism is strikingly egalitarian—each person's happiness counts equally—and radically consequentialist: intentions and duties matter only insofar as they produce good outcomes. Though controversial, as it can justify harming innocents if aggregate happiness increases, utilitarianism has profoundly influenced moral philosophy, public policy, economics, and contemporary effective altruism.

Jeremy Bentham, living from seventeen forty-eight to eighteen thirty-two, invented utilitarian ethics and argued that morality rests on the principle of utility: maximizing pleasure and minimizing pain. John Stuart Mill, from eighteen hundred six to eighteen seventy-three, refined utilitarianism by distinguishing higher and lower pleasures, with mental pleasures superior to physical ones. Henry Sidgwick, from eighteen thirty-eight to nineteen hundred, systematized utilitarianism and exposed what he called the dualism of practical reason—the tension between self-interest and altruism.

The greatest happiness principle holds that the right act maximizes overall happiness or well-being and that we should evaluate acts by their consequences, not by our motives. Impartiality demands that each person's happiness counts equally with no privileging of oneself or one's tribe. Act utilitarians maximize utility case by case, while rule utilitarians follow rules such as honesty and justice that generally maximize utility. Yet utilitarianism faces persistent objections. It appears demandingly to require enormous sacrifice, such as donating all surplus to aid organizations. It struggles to accommodate why you should prioritize your own projects and relationships, and it seems to permit harming the innocent. Modern variants include preference utilitarianism, negative utilitarianism which minimizes suffering, and two-level utilitarianism developed by Hare.

Utilitarianism emerged during industrialization and political reform, offering a principle that transcended tradition and prejudice: pursue the greatest happiness for the greatest number. It grounded positions radical for its time, including women's suffrage and animal welfare, in a single secular principle. Utilitarianism became the language of policy analysis and economics through cost-benefit analysis and welfare economics. Its assumption that well-being is the ultimate value remains dominant in contemporary ethics even among non-utilitarians. Effective altruism, artificial intelligence alignment research, and global health prioritization all invoke utilitarian reasoning.
